2026-W33.question: What do we owe the people who come after us?
2026-W33.premise: Almost every decision in a resource region is really a decision about time — a cutblock, a tailings pond, a municipal debt, an archive nobody funds, a language with four fluent speakers left. Some traditions formalise the obligation across generations; most institutions discount it to nearly zero. The question is what a duty to people who cannot yet object actually requires, and who is willing to pay for it now.

2026-W34.question: Why is everyone in tech so sad?
2026-W34.premise: An emotional recession has settled over knowledge work — layoffs, AI anxiety, and the collapse of the mission-driven self-image that carried the industry for two decades. The people who were supposed to be building the future increasingly describe their own work as pointless. The open question is what happens to a society when an entire class of workers loses faith in its careers, and whether the trades, the land, and the small-town economies that were told to envy that class have something to say back.

2026-W35.question: Who is allowed to fix things?
2026-W35.premise: Fixing something requires permission as often as it requires skill — a warranty, a licence, a certification, a proprietary diagnostic tool, a professional body, a funding body that recognises only certain credentials. Rural places have always repaired what cities replace, and are now told they may not. The question is where the line between gatekeeping and genuine competence actually falls, and who gets to draw it.

2026-W36.question: Is it better to be self-sufficient or well-connected?
2026-W36.premise: Rural identity leans hard on independence — your own water, your own power, your own woodpile, your own read on the weather. But almost every rural success story turns out to run on a network: a co-op, a mutual aid list, a shared mill, a partnership agreement, a satellite dish. The question is whether self-sufficiency is a genuine strategy or a story people tell about infrastructure they've stopped noticing.

2026-W37.question: What gets lost when something gets easier?
2026-W37.premise: Every tool that removes friction also removes the practice that friction produced — reading a map, reading a river, reading a room, knowing a stand of timber by walking it. Sometimes what's lost was drudgery worth losing. Sometimes it was the only way the knowledge was ever transmitted. The question is how to tell the two apart before the last person who had the skill retires.

2026-W38.question: Who decides what's worth saving?
2026-W38.premise: Not everything survives, and the choosing is rarely explicit. A species gets recovery funding or doesn't; a building gets heritage status or a demolition permit; a mill town gets a transition plan or a highway sign; a dialect gets documented or doesn't. The question is who is actually in the room when those calls get made, and what happens to the things nobody nominated.

2026-W39.question: Does a place still exist if nobody records it?
2026-W39.premise: The Cariboo is thinly documented and getting thinner — a shrinking local press, council meetings nobody minutes, oral history held by people in their eighties, ecosystems monitored by satellite but not by anyone who lives there. Meanwhile the same landscape is captured in enormous detail by systems that answer to nobody local. The question is what the difference is between being recorded and being known.

2026-W40.question: When is small genuinely better, and when is it just an excuse?
2026-W40.premise: Small is the region's default virtue — small mills, small farms, small classrooms, small government. Sometimes small really does mean responsive, repairable, and accountable. Sometimes it means underfunded, unaccountable, and one retirement away from collapse, defended with the language of virtue. The question is which one you're looking at, and how you'd know.

framings.0: Test whether a small-town arts festival or community radio station running on three volunteers is nimble and authentic, or one grant rejection away from folding entirely.
framings.1: Weigh whether a small independent logging contractor or family ranch surviving without new equipment is resourceful stewardship, or a safety and viability gap the big licensees no longer have to own.
framings.2: Ask whether the homelab hobbyist or one-truck repair shop fixing gear instead of replacing it is genuine self-reliance, or a workaround for the parts and service the region can no longer get delivered.
framings.3: Examine whether a small, community-run language or land-monitoring program is the right scale for Tŝilhqot'in, Secwépemc, or Dakelh governance, or a chronic underfunding that outside agencies count on to stay convenient.
framings.4: Question whether a small volunteer search-and-rescue or backcountry patrol crew is the fitting size for Chilcotin wilderness, or a thin, exhausted line standing between wildfire season and disaster.
framings.5: Press whether Williams Lake council, SD27, or a Bella Coola improvement district keeping things small and local means real accountability, or just too few staff and dollars to do the job asked of them.
framings.6: Consider whether a small local citizen-science or monitoring project tracking Cariboo ecology yields real, usable knowledge, or is too thin a dataset to tell us anything the region can act on.

2026-W41.question: What are we actually measuring?
2026-W41.premise: Timber volume is not forest health. Test scores are not learning. Attendance is not participation. Engagement is not attention. Every institution runs on a number that stands in for something it cannot count directly, and over time the proxy quietly becomes the goal. The question is what each of our numbers was originally supposed to be about, and how far it has drifted.

framings.0: When a festival or gallery grant is judged by ticket counts and tourism dollars, what gets lost that a Williams Lake audience would actually value, and should arts funders keep counting at all?
framings.1: Allowable annual cut and cubic metres harvested drive Cariboo forestry policy, yet mill closures continue, so ask what those volumes never captured about fibre quality, jobs, and whether the forest is healthy.
framings.2: Spec sheets and star ratings sell the gear, but on a ranch with spotty signal and a tight budget, what should we measure instead to know a gadget or homelab build is worth owning?
framings.3: Count of fluent speakers and signed agreements are how language revitalization and governance get reported, so ask what Tŝilhqot'in, Secwépemc, and Dakelh communities would count instead to know their stewardship is working.
framings.4: Hectares burned and evacuation numbers define each wildfire season, but what do they hide about backcountry recovery, ranch and trail losses, and who actually carries the cost of a bad year?
framings.5: Council and school board reports lean on permits issued, enrolment, and attendance, so ask which local numbers in Williams Lake, Quesnel, or 100 Mile House have drifted furthest from the everyday life they claim to track.
framings.6: Species counts, snowpack readings, and salmon returns anchor Cariboo science stories, yet each is a stand-in, so ask what researchers truly cannot count directly and whether we are ever tempted to treat the proxy as the ecosystem.

generated.question: Who gets to call themselves local?
generated.premise: Small places run on a quiet sorting of who belongs, and the rules are never written down. Length of residence, family name, land ownership, showing up to the work, and simply staying through bad winters all compete as claims. Newcomers often carry the energy and money that keep a town alive, while old-timers carry the history and the right to feel crowded out. It is hard to say whether belonging is something you inherit, something you earn, or something a place decides for itself.

generated.question: When is keeping the peace worth more than being right?
generated.premise: In a place where you will meet the same people at the post office, the rink, and the funeral for decades, every disagreement carries a long tail. Swallowing a complaint can protect a neighbour, a working relationship, or a fragile committee. It can also let a bad practice, a quiet injustice, or a dangerous shortcut carry on for years. Whether silence is a form of care or a form of cowardice often only becomes clear in hindsight, and sometimes not even then.

generated.question: Is it fair to help the people who are already helping?
generated.premise: Rural life runs on favours, volunteer hours, and informal credit, and those who give the most tend to be the first called on and the first looked after. That keeps the web of obligation alive and rewards real contribution. It also leaves out the person who is new, shy, sick, or simply unable to give back. We disagree about whether help is a debt repaid or a gift that should reach people regardless of what they have put in.

generated.question: How much should neighbours know about each other?
generated.premise: Everyone notices whose truck is in the yard, whose lights are on late, and whose marriage is struggling. That watchfulness is also what gets a stranded driver found, a failing elder checked on, and a theft noticed. But it is the same attention that fuels gossip, judgment, and the feeling of never being able to start over. Where care ends and surveillance begins depends on who is looking and what they intend to do with what they see.

generated.question: Is staying put a virtue or a failure of nerve?
generated.premise: Some people stay because the land, the family, and the work are the point, and holding a place together takes someone willing to hold still. Others stay because leaving was frightening, expensive, or never seriously imagined. Those who go often send back money, ideas, and a wider view, though they also take young talent and leave thinner communities behind. It is hard to know from the outside whether a given decision to stay or go is courage, habit, or fear.

generated.question: Who should carry the risk when something goes wrong?
generated.premise: Out where help is hours away, a bad road, a late fire season, a failed crop, or a backcountry mistake lands on someone, and the question of who is responsible gets tangled fast. Individuals are expected to look after themselves, yet institutions, employers, landowners, and whole towns end up absorbing the cost. Pushing risk onto the person closest to it preserves freedom and keeps decisions local. Spreading it out is gentler and fairer, but it can make everyone more careless and more dependent. We disagree about where the line sits between your problem and ours.
